screens.title: Cryptographic Hashing and Digital Signatures
screens.narratorSegment: In enterprise security, we must distinguish three related primitives that protect data in different ways: cryptographic hashes, Message Authentication Codes, and digital signatures. A cryptographic hash reduces any data to a fixed-size digest that is sensitive to tiny changes, making it excellent for integrity checks but not for proving who created the data. A MAC adds a shared secret to provide both integrity and authenticity between two parties. A digital signature uses asymmetric keys and adds non-repudiation, proving both origin and integrity to many recipients without shared secrets. In this lesson you will learn the properties of each primitive, how verification works in practice, and why weak hashes like MD5 and SHA-1 must be retired. We will walk through a verification example with detached signatures and a hands-on file-hashing exercise to see the avalanche effect. By the end you will know when to use a hash, a MAC, or a signature, how to verify a signature with common tools, and how to plan for algorithm migration to maintain long-term security.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Cryptographic Hashing and Digital Signatures

Practical patterns for verifying integrity, authenticating origin, and preventing repudiation in enterprise systems.

In this lesson

Understand hashing, MACs, and signatures and how to verify them with common tools.

Why it matters

Selecting the wrong primitive can break security for distributed updates, legal documents, and protocol authentication.

Core idea
Hash = integrity; MAC = integrity + authenticity using a secret; Signature = integrity + authenticity + non-repudiation using public/private keys.
Outcome
Decide which primitive to use for updates, APIs, and signed documents.
Explore Key Topics
Hashing
Fixed-size digests and the avalanche effect used for integrity checks.
MACs
Shared-secret authentication using HMAC for point-to-point trust.
Signatures
Public-key signatures provide non-repudiation and broad verification.
Visual Concept
Digest flows
Input produces digest. Add secret for MAC. Sign digest with private key for signature.
Quick note
Hashes alone do not prove origin. Use signatures when recipients must independently verify origin without a shared secret.
Key Takeaway

Choose the primitive that provides the properties you need: integrity, authenticity, or non-repudiation. Plan to replace weak hashes and design systems for algorithm agility.

screens.title: Cryptographic Hashing and its Properties
screens.narratorSegment: A cryptographic hash function maps data of any size to a fixed-size digest. The function is one-way: you cannot recover the original input from the digest. Key security properties are preimage resistance, second preimage resistance, and collision resistance. Preimage resistance prevents an attacker from finding an input that matches a given digest. Second preimage resistance prevents finding a different input that matches the digest of a specific message. Collision resistance prevents finding any two distinct inputs with the same digest. In practice this means a small edit produces a radically different digest — the avalanche effect. As a concrete example, computing SHA-256 over a file and then changing one character will result in an entirely different hash. A common misconception is to treat a hash as a signature; a raw hash proves integrity only if the digest itself is trusted. If an attacker can replace both a file and its published hash, the check fails. Use hashes for local integrity checks, file deduplication, and fast comparisons, but not to prove origin by themselves. Key takeaway: hashes detect changes reliably, but authenticity requires an additional secret or asymmetric mechanism.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Cryptographic Hashing
Definition

Properties of cryptographic hashes

A one-way mapping to a fixed-size digest with important resistance properties used to detect alteration.

Key properties
  • Preimage resistance: hard to find an input for a given digest.
  • Second preimage resistance: hard to find a different input with same digest as a target file.
  • Collision resistance: hard to find any two inputs with the same digest.
Concrete example

Compute SHA-256 for a file, edit one character, compute again — the two digests will be completely different because of the avalanche effect.

Common mistake

Trusting a published digest without ensuring the digest itself is authenticated can lead to a false sense of security.

Example — SHA-256
openssl dgst -sha256 original_document.txt
# returns a 64 byte hex digest for the file
Run the command before and after a small change to observe how drastically the hex output changes.
Key Takeaway

Use hashes to detect modification, not to assert who made a change. For origin, use a MAC or a signature.

screens.title: Hash vs MAC vs Digital Signature
screens.narratorSegment: These three primitives overlap but provide different guarantees. A hash gives integrity by producing a digest sensitive to changes, but it does not provide authenticity because anyone can compute the digest. A Message Authentication Code combines a secret key and the message to produce a tag, giving both integrity and authenticity, but it requires the sender and receiver to share the secret key. HMAC is a standard construction that uses a hash function and a secret key to make a strong MAC. Digital signatures use asymmetric keys: the signer creates a signature with a private key and recipients verify with the public key. This provides integrity and authenticity at scale and adds non-repudiation because only the private key holder could create that signature. For example, an update server that must distribute software to thousands of clients should use digital signatures rather than a MAC so each client can verify with a public key. A common misconception is that a MAC is always superior because it uses a secret; in reality, MACs are ideal for point-to-point channels but unsuitable for open distribution where no shared secret exists. The right choice depends on who needs to verify and whether non-repudiation is required.

keyIdea.title: Choosing a primitive
keyIdea.text: Select MACs for shared-secret channels; use signatures for public verification and non-repudiation; use hashes only for local integrity checks.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Hash vs MAC vs Signature
Comparison

Guarantees compared

Cryptographic Hash
Integrity only. Fast to compute. Anyone can create a digest. Use for detecting accidental or malicious changes when the digest itself is protected.
Message Authentication Code (MAC)
Integrity and authenticity for parties sharing a secret key. Efficient and suitable for internal APIs. HMAC is a common construction.
Digital Signature
Integrity, authenticity, and non-repudiation using asymmetric keys. Ideal for software distribution and legally binding documents because it does not require a shared secret.
Use-case cards
Software distribution

Use digital signatures so each client can verify using the vendor's public key without sharing secrets.

API communication

Use HMAC for integrity and authenticity between two internal services that share a secret key.

Local integrity checks

Use hashes for quick integrity checks, deduplication, and as inputs to MACs or signatures.

Misconception

A MAC is not a drop-in replacement for a signature in distributed systems because it requires pre-shared secrets with every verifier.

screens.title: How HMAC Works
screens.narratorSegment: A Hash-based Message Authentication Code (HMAC) uses a cryptographic hash function together with a secret key to produce a tag that authenticates a message. The sender and receiver both share a secret key. To create an HMAC, the sender combines the secret with the message according to the HMAC construction and computes the hash; the resulting tag travels with the message. The receiver performs the same operation with the shared key and compares the computed tag to the received tag. If they match, the receiver gains confidence that the message wasn't altered and that the sender knows the shared secret. A concrete example is two internal services where service A sends a JSON payload with an HMAC header computed using a shared secret; service B recalculates the tag and validates it before processing. A common mistake is reusing a key across many systems without rotation; compromise of the key destroys all authenticity guarantees. Also avoid using plain hashes with a secret concatenated in an ad-hoc way; use HMAC constructions from established libraries. How HMAC Works means hmac provides efficient, secret-key-based authenticity and integrity for point-to-point channels when a shared secret can be safely maintained.. In practical terms, shared-secret authentication using hash functions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › HMAC Process
Process

Creating and verifying an HMAC

1
Sender computes tag
Combine message and secret using the HMAC construction and compute the hash-based tag.
2
Sender sends message + tag
Tag is appended as a header or trailer; transport must protect confidentiality if needed, but tag itself authenticates integrity.
3
Receiver verifies
Receiver recomputes HMAC with the shared key and compares tags; match confirms integrity and authenticity.
Concrete example

An internal API includes an HMAC header computed over the JSON payload using a secret stored in each service's secrets manager. The verifying service rejects requests with mismatched tags.

Pro tip
Rotate shared keys regularly, store secrets in a managed vault, and prefer library HMAC implementations rather than homegrown constructions.
Pitfall

Using the same secret across many services increases blast radius if the secret is leaked; plan per-service keys and rotation policies.

Key Takeaway

HMAC gives efficient integrity and authenticity for shared-secret scenarios; it is not suitable for public verification at scale.

screens.title: Digital Signatures: Principles and Guarantees
screens.narratorSegment: Digital signatures use asymmetric cryptography to sign a digest of the message with a private key. The recipient uses the signer's public key to verify that the signature is valid and that the hash of the received message matches the decrypted digest. This yields three critical guarantees: integrity — the message has not been altered since signing; authenticity — the signer controls the private key and therefore is the claimed origin; and non-repudiation — the signer cannot later credibly deny having signed because only they possess the private key. A concrete scenario is code signing: the vendor signs an installer with their private key. Any client with the vendor's public key can verify the signature and trust the installer. A common misconception is believing that possession of a public key is enough to verify identity; the public key must be obtained through a trusted channel or certificate authority, otherwise an attacker could substitute a fraudulent public key. Key takeaway: digital signatures scale verification and provide legal and operational accountability when keys and trust anchors are properly managed. Digital Signatures: Principles and Guarantees means signatures prove origin and integrity and support non-repudiation when private keys are protected and public keys are trusted.. In practical terms, asymmetric signing for authenticity, integrity, and non-repudiation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Digital Signatures
Definition

How signing and verification work

Sign with private key → verifier checks with public key and recomputes hash to compare.

Practical guarantees
  • Integrity: tampering breaks verification.
  • Authenticity: signature ties content to a private key owner.
  • Non-repudiation: the signer cannot credibly deny the signature later.
Concrete example

A vendor signs software installers. Each client verifies the signature with the vendor's trusted public key before installing to ensure origin and integrity.

Trust note
The trustworthiness of a signature depends on how the public key is distributed. Use certificates and trusted channels to bind public keys to identities.
Misconception

A valid signature does not imply the signer is trustworthy; it only confirms that the signed content came from the private key holder. Separate trust policies are required.

Key Takeaway

Use signatures for broad verification and legal/non-repudiation needs, and manage key protection and trust anchors carefully.

screens.title: Signing and Verifying with GPG
screens.narratorSegment: GPG is commonly used to create detached signatures for files. The high-level process is: generate or use an existing key pair, sign the file to produce a detached signature, and distribute the file and signature. Recipients run verification against the signature and the file. A concrete example: create a simple text file, run a detached sign operation to produce a. sig or. asc file, and then verify that signature against the file. When verification succeeds, GPG confirms both the signature's validity and which key made the signature. A common misconception is trusting a signature without verifying the public key; verification requires that the recipient has the signer's public key from a trusted source or a certificate authority chain. In practice, package maintainers publish their public keys through trusted channels and often sign release manifests so clients can validate package integrity before installation. The key operational step is to ensure public keys are authenticated and to treat keys as critical assets that require rotation and revocation plans. Signing and Verifying with GPG means use detached signatures for files, and always verify signatures against a trusted public key to confirm origin.. In practical terms, detached signatures for distributed verification. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › GPG Signing
Code Walkthrough

Detached signing and verification

# Create a sample file
echo "This document is confidential." > document.txt

# Create a detached signature
# gpg --output document.txt.sig --detach-sign document.txt

# Verify the detached signature
# gpg --verify document.txt.sig document.txt
Run the commands in a terminal. The verify step reports whether the signature matches and which key produced it. If the public key is not trusted, GPG indicates the key's status; obtain the public key from a trusted source before accepting the signature.
Concrete scenario

When downloading a distribution iso, a detached PGP signature allows independent verification that the ISO file matches the vendor-signed digest before installation.

Trust reminder

Ensure you obtain the signer's public key through a trusted channel and check key fingerprints to avoid key substitution attacks.

Key Takeaway

Detached signatures let recipients verify files independently; always validate the public key's provenance.

screens.title: Signature Algorithms: RSA and ECDSA
screens.narratorSegment: Two widely used families of signature algorithms are RSA and Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm, or ECDSA. RSA relies on the difficulty of factoring large integers, while ECDSA relies on elliptic curve discrete logarithms. RSA keys are typically larger for a given security level, which can increase signature size and computation time. ECDSA achieves comparable security with smaller keys and signatures, which is attractive for constrained devices and bandwidth-sensitive systems. In practice, the choice often depends on implementation requirements and ecosystem compatibility. For example, older systems may expect RSA-signed certificates, while newer systems may prefer ECDSA for performance. A common misconception is thinking smaller keys always reduce security; in elliptic-curve algorithms, carefully chosen curves provide strong security with smaller key sizes. Key takeaway: select algorithms based on security, performance, and interoperability, and maintain the ability to transition algorithms as standards evolve. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › RSA vs ECDSA
Comparison

RSA

Based on integer factorization. Well-supported and broadly compatible, but larger keys and signatures for a given security level.

Example use

Legacy PKI deployments and systems requiring broad support.

Comparison

ECDSA

Uses elliptic curve discrete logarithm problems. Smaller keys and signatures with comparable security, good for constrained environments.

Example use

Mobile devices, IoT, and modern TLS deployments prioritizing performance and smaller certificates.

Operational note

Ensure your key management and certificate provisioning processes support the algorithm you choose, and design for agility to migrate algorithms when necessary.

screens.title: Hash Collisions and Weak Algorithms
screens.narratorSegment: A hash collision occurs when two different inputs produce the same digest. Collision resistance is a fundamental property of secure hash functions. When collisions are practically achievable, an attacker can craft a malicious input that shares a digest with a legitimate file, undermining integrity checks. MD5 and SHA-1 have known collision attacks, which is why they are deprecated for security-critical uses such as digital signatures and password hashing. A common example used in practice is creating two files with the same MD5 digest so a signed document and a malicious variant appear identical by digest alone. The operational implication is clear: systems using MD5 or SHA-1 for signatures or other trust decisions must migrate to stronger families such as SHA-2 or SHA-3. A misconception is that salting or other techniques always fix weak hashes; while salting helps against precomputed tables, it does not restore collision resistance. Key takeaway: treat MD5 and SHA-1 as broken for security purposes and plan migrations with compatibility and signature re-issuance in mind. Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Hash Collisions
Definition

What is a collision?

Two distinct inputs that produce the same hash digest. This breaks collision resistance and can allow content substitution attacks.

Historical note

MD5 and SHA-1 have documented collision attacks. Do not use them for security-critical tasks like signing or password hashing.

Concrete implication

If a vendor signs a file using a weak hash, an attacker could create a malicious file with the same digest and present it as authentic; verification would be deceptive.

Mitigation
Migrate systems to SHA-2 or SHA-3, plan certificate and artifact re-signing, and design cryptographic agility so algorithms can be updated without service disruption.
Action

Inventory places where MD5 or SHA-1 are used and prioritize updates for digital signatures, code signing, and password storage systems.

Key Takeaway

Treat MD5 and SHA-1 as broken for trust decisions. Replace them and design systems to adapt to future algorithm changes.

screens.title: Designing for Cryptographic Agility
screens.narratorSegment: Cryptographic agility is the practice of designing systems so algorithms can be replaced with minimal disruption. Key elements include using modular libraries that accept algorithm identifiers, versioning signatures and digests, maintaining multiple verification paths during transitions, and planning key rotation and certificate re-issuance. A concrete approach is to publish both SHA-256 and SHA-512 digests during migration, allowing clients to accept either while older components update. Avoid hardcoding algorithm names into binaries or protocols. A common mistake is assuming a single update will cover every dependent system; instead, map dependencies and stage rollouts. Also plan for revocation and compromise scenarios so you can rapidly invalidate affected keys and reissue signatures. The operational benefit is resilience: when a vulnerability is discovered in a hash or signature algorithm, an agile system can adopt the replacement algorithm quickly, minimizing exposure and preserving trust for distributed consumers. screens.title: Hands-on: Observe the SHA-256 Avalanche
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity demonstrates how a single character changes a cryptographic digest dramatically. Start by creating a small text file and computing its SHA-256 digest with openssl. Next, change a single character — such as capitalizing a letter — and compute the digest again. You will see a completely different hex string, which is the avalanche effect in action. This proves that even tiny modifications are detectable. The activity is safe and illustrative; you do not need to create collisions. A common misstake is expecting only small digest changes; instead, the entire output changes unpredictably. Use this technique in audits and scripts to assert file integrity before acceptance or deployment. fullNarratorScript:
In enterprise security, we must distinguish three related primitives that protect data in different ways: cryptographic hashes, Message Authentication Codes, and digital signatures. A cryptographic hash reduces any data to a fixed-size digest that is sensitive to tiny changes, making it excellent for integrity checks but not for proving who created the data. A MAC adds a shared secret to provide both integrity and authenticity between two parties. A digital signature uses asymmetric keys and adds non-repudiation, proving both origin and integrity to many recipients without shared secrets. In this lesson you will learn the properties of each primitive, how verification works in practice, and why weak hashes like MD5 and SHA-1 must be retired. We will walk through a verification example with detached signatures and a hands-on file-hashing exercise to see the avalanche effect. By the end you will know when to use a hash, a MAC, or a signature, how to verify a signature with common tools, and how to plan for algorithm migration to maintain long-term security.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to tell when to use a cryptographic hash, a Message Authentication Code, and a digital signature. You will understand how each primitive protects integrity and whether it proves origin. You will also be able to implement and verify signatures with common tools, and to explain why weak hashes must be deprecated. Each objective pairs a cognitive skill with a real operational outcome. For example, differentiating hashes, MACs, and signatures means you can design an update distribution process that uses signatures for broad verification rather than a shared secret. Explaining digital signatures means you can audit code signing processes for authenticity and non-repudiation. Implementing verification procedures shows you can configure gpg or equivalent tools to confirm software or document provenance. Finally, analyzing collision risks and recommending migration paths equips you to create cryptographic-agile systems that can replace vulnerable algorithms without disruptive overhauls. These skills protect software delivery, legal documents, and critical enterprise communications.

These applied objectives show what you will do in practice. You will implement and verify a detached signature and interpret verification output so you can accept or reject a file. You will run a file hash before and after a minor change to observe the avalanche effect and use that evidence to argue for integrity controls. You will evaluate an existing system that uses MD5 or SHA-1 and produce a migration plan that prioritizes software distribution channels and certificate chains. Finally, you will compare symmetric MACs and asymmetric signatures to choose a design for internal services versus public distribution. Each objective links a testable action to a security outcome. For example, verifying a detached gpg signature demonstrates both integrity and origin for open distribution, while using HMAC protects internal point-to-point APIs where shared secrets are feasible. These skills make your audits and architecture designs defensible and repeatable.

A cryptographic hash function maps data of any size to a fixed-size digest. The function is one-way: you cannot recover the original input from the digest. Key security properties are preimage resistance, second preimage resistance, and collision resistance. Preimage resistance prevents an attacker from finding an input that matches a given digest. Second preimage resistance prevents finding a different input that matches the digest of a specific message. Collision resistance prevents finding any two distinct inputs with the same digest. In practice this means a small edit produces a radically different digest — the avalanche effect. As a concrete example, computing SHA-256 over a file and then changing one character will result in an entirely different hash. A common misconception is to treat a hash as a signature; a raw hash proves integrity only if the digest itself is trusted. If an attacker can replace both a file and its published hash, the check fails. Use hashes for local integrity checks, file deduplication, and fast comparisons, but not to prove origin by themselves. Key takeaway: hashes detect changes reliably, but authenticity requires an additional secret or asymmetric mechanism.

These three primitives overlap but provide different guarantees. A hash gives integrity by producing a digest sensitive to changes, but it does not provide authenticity because anyone can compute the digest. A Message Authentication Code combines a secret key and the message to produce a tag, giving both integrity and authenticity, but it requires the sender and receiver to share the secret key. HMAC is a standard construction that uses a hash function and a secret key to make a strong MAC. Digital signatures use asymmetric keys: the signer creates a signature with a private key and recipients verify with the public key. This provides integrity and authenticity at scale and adds non-repudiation because only the private key holder could create that signature. For example, an update server that must distribute software to thousands of clients should use digital signatures rather than a MAC so each client can verify with a public key. A common misconception is that a MAC is always superior because it uses a secret; in reality, MACs are ideal for point-to-point channels but unsuitable for open distribution where no shared secret exists. The right choice depends on who needs to verify and whether non-repudiation is required.

A Hash-based Message Authentication Code (HMAC) uses a cryptographic hash function together with a secret key to produce a tag that authenticates a message. The sender and receiver both share a secret key. To create an HMAC, the sender combines the secret with the message according to the HMAC construction and computes the hash; the resulting tag travels with the message. The receiver performs the same operation with the shared key and compares the computed tag to the received tag. If they match, the receiver gains confidence that the message wasn't altered and that the sender knows the shared secret. A concrete example is two internal services where service A sends a JSON payload with an HMAC header computed using a shared secret; service B recalculates the tag and validates it before processing. A common mistake is reusing a key across many systems without rotation; compromise of the key destroys all authenticity guarantees. Also avoid using plain hashes with a secret concatenated in an ad-hoc way; use HMAC constructions from established libraries. How HMAC Works means hmac provides efficient, secret-key-based authenticity and integrity for point-to-point channels when a shared secret can be safely maintained.. In practical terms, shared-secret authentication using hash functions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Digital signatures use asymmetric cryptography to sign a digest of the message with a private key. The recipient uses the signer's public key to verify that the signature is valid and that the hash of the received message matches the decrypted digest. This yields three critical guarantees: integrity — the message has not been altered since signing; authenticity — the signer controls the private key and therefore is the claimed origin; and non-repudiation — the signer cannot later credibly deny having signed because only they possess the private key. A concrete scenario is code signing: the vendor signs an installer with their private key. Any client with the vendor's public key can verify the signature and trust the installer. A common misconception is believing that possession of a public key is enough to verify identity; the public key must be obtained through a trusted channel or certificate authority, otherwise an attacker could substitute a fraudulent public key. Key takeaway: digital signatures scale verification and provide legal and operational accountability when keys and trust anchors are properly managed. GPG is commonly used to create detached signatures for files. The high-level process is: generate or use an existing key pair, sign the file to produce a detached signature, and distribute the file and signature. Recipients run verification against the signature and the file. A concrete example: create a simple text file, run a detached sign operation to produce a. sig or. asc file, and then verify that signature against the file. When verification succeeds, GPG confirms both the signature's validity and which key made the signature. A common misconception is trusting a signature without verifying the public key; verification requires that the recipient has the signer's public key from a trusted source or a certificate authority chain. In practice, package maintainers publish their public keys through trusted channels and often sign release manifests so clients can validate package integrity before installation. The key operational step is to ensure public keys are authenticated and to treat keys as critical assets that require rotation and revocation plans. Two widely used families of signature algorithms are RSA and Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm, or ECDSA. RSA relies on the difficulty of factoring large integers, while ECDSA relies on elliptic curve discrete logarithms. RSA keys are typically larger for a given security level, which can increase signature size and computation time. ECDSA achieves comparable security with smaller keys and signatures, which is attractive for constrained devices and bandwidth-sensitive systems. In practice, the choice often depends on implementation requirements and ecosystem compatibility. For example, older systems may expect RSA-signed certificates, while newer systems may prefer ECDSA for performance. Cryptographic agility is the practice of designing systems so algorithms can be replaced with minimal disruption. Key elements include using modular libraries that accept algorithm identifiers, versioning signatures and digests, maintaining multiple verification paths during transitions, and planning key rotation and certificate re-issuance. Imagine you must distribute critical software updates to remote servers and ensure both integrity and that updates originate from your trusted build system. The correct choice is digital signatures. Use the build system's private key to sign each update artifact, publish the artifact and signature, and distribute the vendor's public key to servers through a trusted channel. Each server verifies the signature before applying the update. A MAC would require sharing secrets with every server and would not provide non-repudiation. A raw hash alone does not prove origin because an attacker could replace both file and published hash. Summarizing the essentials: a cryptographic hash provides a compact integrity check but no origin proof; a Message Authentication Code combines a secret with a hash to provide integrity and authenticity between parties sharing a key; a digital signature uses private keys to sign a hash and public keys to verify, giving integrity, authenticity, and non-repudiation. Be aware that MD5 and SHA-1 are deprecated because collision attacks are practicable, and always prefer SHA-2 or SHA-3 families for security-critical uses. For practical workflows, use HMACs for internal shared-secret channels and digital signatures for public distribution and code signing. Finally, design cryptographic agility into systems so you can transition to new algorithms without breaking verification. These concepts will guide secure design and auditing choices across software distribution, document signing, and secure communications. Keep three practical rules in mind. First, treat hashes as integrity indicators only; they do not authenticate origin. Second, use HMAC for authenticating messages between parties that can securely share a secret. Third, use digital signatures when you need public verification and non-repudiation for software, documents, or widespread distribution. Additionally, inventory any systems using MD5 or SHA-1 and plan their replacement with SHA-2 or SHA-3. Finally, protect signing private keys, authenticate public keys through trusted channels, and design your system to support future algorithm changes. These simple practices will make your integrity and authentication architecture resilient and auditable.
